items.heading: COMMENT
items.summary: Editorial noting a quiet winter apart from the Christchurch representatives, welcoming the new club coaching set-up and the growing number of young members, and calling for broad support to lift Belgrave to the top of athletics.
items.text:
COMMENT

Christchurch representatives apart, we have had a rather quiet winter season in all sections but the long awaited inception of a Club coaching set-up heralds exciting times ahead.

Many youngsters have been attracted to Belgrave Harriers in the past twelve months and we now find that twenty-nine per cent of our members are under the age of twenty-one, and hopefully that percentage will be pushed a lot higher still. Only a relatively small number will become champions but good coaching and an interest shown in the development of our youngsters by older members will maintain their enthusiasm for the sport of athletics and spread the word that ours is a Club that can provide the facilities they need. The broader we can make our base of solid Club athletes, the more stars we will produce to lead our teams and take us through the rest of the 'seventies' and beyond.

It is not a miracle that we need to put Belgrave at the very top of athletics instead of its middle reaches, just hard work. Hard work that has been begun and which now needs as many broad shoulders as possible to share the load and make our movement upwards irresistible.

items.heading: grapevine
items.summary: Club news column: Charlie Smart's illness, Bernard Eglington's marriage, Gordon Doubleday's poor health, Hall cleaning, New Zealand Belgravians, Alf Taylor, a donor's letter, Surrey County AAA posts, Ed. Lacey's commended photograph, Derek Crookes as new Belgrave '20' organiser, membership of 469, Linda Manning's raffle sales and a wedding rumour.
items.text:
grapevine

Unfortunately CHARLIE SMART suffered a setback recently in his fight back to good health and he is unable at present to get out of the house. Visitors would be more than welcome at his home - 25 Borneo Street, SW15. Meanwhile, all the best Charlie, and may we soon see you about once again.

Congratulations to Vice-President BERNARD EGLINGTON upon his recent marriage. He joined the Club about thirty years ago when he was a full time member of the R.A.F., and was previously with Derby & County. He made the switch from running to walking and soon made his mark over the longer distances and figured in many of our winning teams. By walking step for step with the late Cyril Yescombe from Brighton to London and back he became Centurion No. 344. Now living in the Colwyn Bay area he keeps himself fit and we are always glad when he makes a trip to town to line up with the Bels team. We wish Bernard and Grace many years of health and happiness.

Unhappy news comes from GORDON DOUBLEDAY. It seems that he is having to take things very quietly at the moment after suffering a patch of bad health. Treatment has consisted of having to sleep sitting up and taking a vast array of pills amongst other things. Let us hope that his recovery is swift and that once again,armed with stop-watch,he will be presiding over the finish of our races.

There is a notice in Belgrave Hall asking for volunteers to clean the Hall. Please add your name to the accompanying list if you are one of those who regularly use our facilities. It might even be worth your while - our Hon. Treasurer (who else) found some loose change whilst Field Events Sec. Bill Couzens even found a couple of old runners under the tables amongst the dust!

Our walkers in New Zealand for the Commonwealth Games met up with two Belgravians from "Down Under" while they were there. DAVE DE BONDI and VIC TOWNSEND both send their regards to all Bels.

It is pleasing to hear (via Harry Shields) that our Past President ALF TAYLOR and his wife JENNY are both well in their Somerset retreat. Alf was a member of our winning E.C.C.U. teams and was also Social Secretary for some time.

An irate letter, using the President's pre-stamped envelope, was returned with 20p and a curt note saying this was not for the appeal as a club like ours didn't ought to have to stoop to this sort of thing - it was for our mag. the "Belgravian". Thank you donor - but are you aware that it barely pays for ONE magazine and postage and you have FOUR each year.

The christmas pudding won in one of our raffles by a Blackheath Harrier was duly consumed by our Kentish friends at a Blackheath supper. ........ ..What's that, you mean we forgot to put in the "special" ingredient.

Congratulations to FRANK JARVIS who was elected President of the Surrey County A.A.A. in February. CLIVE SHIPPEN and GORDON BISCOE were voted onto the "Surrey" committee.

The work of ED. LACEY, a member since 1948 and whose photographs have appeared in the "Belgravian" for many years, was highly commended in the Sports Picture of the Year category in a competition promoted jointly by the Sports Council and the Royal Photographic Society.

GRAPEVINE continued ....

Good to see ARTHUR PENSTONE jogging again after the operation on one of his achilles tendons.

It is very pleasing to see that a new Race Organiser for the Belgrave '20' has stepped forward. DEREK CROOKES, once our Road Running Secretary, is taking over this year so the continuance of our popular event is once more assured.

We now have 469 members made up as follows:- 298 Seniors, 35 Juniors, 27 Youths, 72 Boys and 37 Honorary members.

Well done LINDA MANNING - only 14 years old and she made over £8 profit sitting for two hours in the cold entrance to our Hall, selling raffle tickets at the Veteran's Southern C.C. Champs. - Made the place look a lot more attractive too.

Finally, the most unlikely rumour reached "Grapevine" in mid-February. It seems that someone is spreading the news that MARIANNE DEW and ALAN BLACK have got themselves hitched and that JOHN BICOURT was best man at the occasion. Of course it couldn't possibly be true .......

items.heading: WHO KNOWS WHERE WE ARE GOING ?
items.summary: Bill Laws questions the purpose of the President's fund-raising appeal, argues Belgrave's performance has declined, and proposes a wider membership with a ladies section, a rebuilt larger clubhouse, appeal funding and a community-club model.
items.text:
Bill Laws writes:-

WHO KNOWS WHERE WE ARE GOING ?

I am sure that all active members were delighted at the choice of our current President and awaited with anticipation the first actions from this energetic man. We soon learned that his self-set task for the year was a fund raising appeal and I, like many others, eagerly responded. However, with the first flush of enthusiasm gone, it occurred to me that the reasons for the fund raising were not clear. Perhaps some new scheme, carefully nurtured but still to see the light of day, was afoot. Certainly rumours had been circulating. The rebuilding of Belgrave Hall was mentioned. The possibility of selling the Hall was being considered and even a deal with the local Council involving new facilities at Wimbledon Park track had been hinted at. The possibilities seemed endless and surely our President's appeal must have some direct relation to one of these plans. But no, re-reading the last "Belgravian" made it clear that the fund raising aims were to improve liquidity and [illegible] provide for a building maintenance fund. So perhaps there were to be no new plans, no new building and certainly no fresh appraisal of where we as a club are going and what our targets for the future should be.

So what about it? How does Belgrave rate as a club now? Are we satisfied with the way things have gone over the last ten years and do we see any need to establish new aims for the future? I should like to see members from all sections of the Club seriously thinking about these matters and the following should stimulate discussion.

During these last few years, which have seen the amalgamation of many clubs, the performance of Belgrave has declined. Fewer trophies, and fewer road and country wins have been the trend. The same old faces have provided stalwart service but where are the new names? We are not attracting and holding enough good youngsters and I believe that we must change our organisation, finances and facilities to compete with many of today's other attractions so here are some proposals:-

1) Widen the membership of the Club. Initiate a ladies section (Yes, I've mentioned the unmentionable). Start a family jogging section and build up a supporters club. Aim for a total membership of several thousand.
2) Re-build, preferably on a larger site, to provide adequate social and recreational facilities for all the groups mentioned above. Provide facilities for additional leisure sports, say table tennis, badminton and squash.
3) Finance these projects initially through an appeal fund but later through increased membership fees and profits from peripheral activities.
4) Make Belgrave a community club and get financial support from local Councils and Government agencies.

By now several members will be pouring their second whisky and soda. But let them consider this. We have modified our role before (remember we were once a boxing club) and we can adjust and expand if we have the desire. In my view we must do this to establish ourselves as the premier athletics club. By introducing the joys of running to a much wider range of people we would attract and hold the membership from which new champions would surely emerge.

WALKING

An uneventful winter season has produced no outstanding performances. In fact it has generally been a depleted Belgrave team that has faced the starting line.

Our last win was in the Belgrave Open when our Commonwealth Games representatives of Lawton, Callow, Duquemin and Moullin were victorious. Our 'B' team was then left to represent us at the subsequent Bexley and Imber Court races.

Out in New Zealand, Carl Lawton won a 10 kilometre event with Alan Callow 3rd and John Moullin 4th, but the main reason for their trip, the 20 miles race at the 'Games' was less productive.

items.heading: BELGRAVE WERE THERE
items.summary: Report on the four Belgrave walkers in the 20 miles walk at the 10th British Commonwealth Games in Christchurch, New Zealand, in January 1974, with the leading and Belgrave placings.
items.text:
BELGRAVE WERE THERE

JANUARY 29th 1974 - CHRISTCHURCH, NEW ZEALAND
THE TENTH BRITISH COMMONWEALTH GAMES

Halfway round the World, Belgrave were well represented in the 10th British Commonwealth Games. The first appearance of our Walkers was in a pre-Games 10 kilometre track event in which they achieved a promising 1, 3, and 4.

The 20 miles Walk was held over an out-and-back course with a 5 p.m. start to avoid the worst of the sun, and of the fifteen starters four were Belgravians, with Len Duquemin and John Moullin for Guernsey, Carl Lawton for England and Allan Callow representing the Isle of Man.

England's Warhurst and Thorpe led all the way. Allan was in the second group for a while but gradually fell off the back. John Moullin was going steadily until the turn when he found the going extremely tough due to the head wind and the cold. Len Duquemin also suffered but it was Carl Lawton who again faded on the big occasion. He was seventh at the turn in 79:25 but slowed drastically before eventually retiring at 14½ miles.

Overall a disappointing result for the Bels but a trip not to be forgotten in a hurry. Other Belgravians making an appearance were Vic Townsend who was 2nd in a veterans race and Dave De Bondi over from Australia to watch.

COACHING

At the last count we had no less than 134 colts, boys, youths and juniors on our books. Of the 335 remaining seniors, no more than a third are active, so with the right efforts we could ensure that the majority of our active members are under 21. What an insurance for the future this would be! However, the under-21's need far more encouragement, attention and coaching than their senior counterparts, for their drop-out rate is higher.

There are many senior members in our club who are not committed to the competition programme and who could contribute tremendously to our efforts with the youngsters. A minor committment to assist would be welcome and, I am sure, would give them much satisfaction. So how about it seniors? Give me a "ring" at 660-0480 and let's talk about it.

o o o

The winter coaching programme got off to a belated start and whilst we have not exactly been over-run with youngsters at least we have established a routine. It is hoped that the future will see no more breaks of contact at the close of the summer season, and that members will appreciate the need to continue through the winter with running and weight training programmes - whatever their event may be. Those who do will have a decided advantage when the next summer season comes around.

o o o

Friday night is weight night. And thanks to the expertise and enthusiasm of BILL COUZENS and JOHN MARTIN has been a success from the outset. The rate of improvement has been most marked and the lads follow their progress sheet with much interest. To provide variety, short, sharp sessions of handball are played; and circuit training has proved to be very popular. Refreshments at the close are as welcome as any after a hard run!

o o o

Although our emphasis has been on the Club's Youth in recent months, the seniors are also able to take advantage of the facilities and equipment. With three sets of weights and dumb-bells at the hall, Tuesday evening is fast becoming the senior's weight training night. Once again, BILL COUZENS and JOHN MARTIN are to the fore in setting the pace.

o o o

Because of our large membership of young athletes the Club has applied for affiliation to the Youth Committee of the London Borough of Merton. Should the Borough decide we are eligible and approve our application, then our membership could well bring us closer still to the Borough's Youth and be of mutual advantage to us both.

o o o

The track and field season fast approaches and our summer training programmes at Battersea Park and Wimbledon Park tracks will be underway before the next issue of the gazette is published. So once again I appeal for volunteers to assist with these programmes; particularly the Sunday morning sessions. The only qualification needed is a keen interest. We need persons who are prepared to time runners, measure throws or supervise jumps By such modest, helpful beginnings are coaches made. Again, let me know if you are interested.

o o o

items.summary: Humorous anecdote about John Bicourt's joke to his wife Val that he would finish his Commonwealth Games race in the nude, and the radio report she later heard about a sensation in the steeplechase.
items.text:
Bicourt threatens to reveal all.....

Before leaving for New Zealand and the Commonwealth Games, John Bicourt told his wife Val that if he found himself likely to come last in his race, he would strip off shorts and singlet and finish the race in the nude. "After all", he said,"I could get more publicity from that than from winning any number of races".

Imagine Val's consternation when listening to the radio on the day of the race....... "And now we go over to Christchurch, New Zealand to hear the latest on the sensation that occurred in the 3000 metres steeplechase."

items.heading: The Festival Of Culture
items.summary: Charles Dabbs's tongue-in-cheek report on President Charles Manning's 'Festival of Culture' stag evening at the club HQ, with a comedian, strippers and a ventriloquist.
items.text:
The Festival Of Culture

CHARLES DABBS (recently fired from the "Longford Committee") REPORTS:-

As I have often been criticized for my infrequent visits to HQ I was grateful to accept the invitation of the well known "impressario" (among other things) and Belgrave President Charles Manning to attend his very discreetly advertized Festival of Culture.

Much to my amazement, on arrival at HQ, I discovered that not only were our own sober gentlemen members in attendance but also the intemperate louts from the other local club which changes its name frequently enough for it to elude me!

With a delay somewhat similar to that at the start of a cross country race your actual culture commenced. A comedian, speaking mostly in very readily understandable vernacular, related some of his experiences to the discerning audience. At one point the writer, commenting on the intellectual appeal of the material, was verbally attacked but managed to survive. Following the comedian, the audience were considerably shocked by the unexpected naked appearance of the female of our species - not normally seen unattired in our revered HQ. The effect of this arrival, followed by another (the President would not, of course, be satisfied by just one - would he?) was to stir the audience into the edging forward of the chairs, the eyes protruding, etc., etc! Not only two naked females but also a ventriloquist's (that's how it's spelt) dummy with an intelligence way above that of some of the runners (especially those of the other club previously referred to) and almost equal to our own!

Eventually, after all the drinking, all the bawdy jokes and all the T's and B's the evening closed as another great Belgrave success. In retrospect, considering the attendance and interest shown, there may well be a future for this type of activity as a regular feature of the revitalized Belgrave Training Programme.

items.summary: Light-hearted account of the club Barn Dance in February, with the 'Swinging Jock Straps' skiffle group, and thanks to Bill and Gwen Couzens, Mrs. Manning and the bar helpers.
items.text:
Barn Dance Frolics

The Barn Dance in February was a great success, although what the country dance band thought of our efforts on the floor is probably better left unsaid.

"Girls to the centre", the caller would cry out. And into the centre amongst the delicately stepping lady friends and wives would troop the stomping John Martin or John Kelly with all the finesse of a couple of pampas bulls.

"Now spin your partner round." Upon which Leo Coy would link arms with Bernard Merry whilst their good ladies could only stand back and laugh helplessly.

Only Eve Stimpson and Bob Taylor seemed to be able to get it all together.

But seriously, one of the most enjoyable things was to get your arm around a girl's waist once again. Those "rave ups" with everyone waving arms and legs .... continued on page 18

BARN DANCE FROLICS continued .......
and rolling their eyes in time to the beat are all very well but let's face it, it's nice once in a while to dance with someone.

The "Swinging Jock Straps", Belgrave's resident skiffle group made another welcome appearance, and their rendition of "My Ol' Man's A Dustman" was enough to make even the most hardened member's eyes come over all misty. Again Bill and Gwen Couzens are owed our gratitude for the arrangements. It takes a lot of hard work to put on an evening such as this. Mrs. Manning, who obviously knows how to feed a hungry athlete, looked after the refreshments, whilst in the bar John Martin did sterling work in ordering the beer, etc., and was ably assisted by Denis MacManus, Jack Carter and Stu. Barrett in the most important job of all - dispensing it to thirsty revellers.

MARCH 5th 1949, SURREY COUNTY 10 MILES ROAD WALK .........
In the Surrey Championship we once again secured double honours, Harry Churcher leading the team in his usual style, followed by Charlie, Mac (Dave McMullen) and Bert East. MARCH 10th 1934, THE "NATIONAL" CROSS COUNTRY, DUDLEY ......
..... Our nine were fairly well away and could be seen battling for their positions in the field of 273 runners as they ran over the first few hundred yards of slightly uphill parkland. ..... At seven miles Burns (Elswick) had increased his lead to one of over 100 yards from Holden (Tipton) and Dodd (Wirral), who were together. Penny had shaken off some of his opposition and was now sixth. Footer seemed to be gaining places throughout the race, having been about 50th when first noticed and now inside the first twenty. Allum and Taylor were running together, about 25th and altogether we had our six in 48 places, including individual runners. .... The finish came in a torrent of rain with our boys totalling 113 points.

Surely, we thought, 113 points is good enough for second team place. Why, this score has won the Championship before now!

A hurried enquiry at the Salford dressing room disclosed that they had scored 112 points.

items.summary: Gordon Biscoe's appeal for helpers at the Belgrave 12 Stage Road Relay at Wimbledon on 6 April, run with the Southern Counties, and for members not to follow the race in cars.
items.text:
ROAD AND COUNTRY

On April 6th, in conjunction with the Southern Counties, we shall once again be holding our 12 Stage Road Relay. This is our biggest promotion of the year and in view of this I would like to take the opportunity of making two important requests.

Firstly, will anyone who can possibly assist on the day, particularly as a pointsman, etc., please contact me as soon as possible. As will be appreciated, several weeks of effort go into staging and making a race such as this a success. All of this effort could be in vain with say one team going off course on the day.

Secondly, over the years we have been continuously faced with the problem of increased traffic on the roads but have so far been very fortunate in having the kind co-operation of the local police. Therefore may I ask all Belgrave members who are present on the day to observe the request printed in the programme. - PLEASE DO NOT FOLLOW THE RACE IN CARS OR CAUSE ANY CONGESTION ON THE ROAD - failure to heed this warning could result in a club being disqualified or even the race being banned - a fate of one road relay already this year! These instructions are issued to all clubs entering the race and as the promoters we must be the first to observe them.

So come to Wimbledon and support your team on April 6th (start is at 12 noon) and enjoy this popular event.

JANUARY 5th 1974 - GUILDFORD

Considerably improving upon last year's performance, the Belgrave team scored a well deserved second place, just edging South London Harriers by two points although a full thirty points down on Hercules Wimbledon. The conditions were atrocious with oceans of mud, a cold wind and even electrified fences to contend with. Our members from north of the Thames have always insisted that the Middlesex race is the toughest on the calendar but even Pat O'Connor, who has now switched his allegiance to Surrey, was heard to utter," The'Middlesex' has never been any worse than this". Gerry North also found it tough but nevertheless it suited him well and he once again qualified for the county team with a splendid run into 5th place. RIMMER TAKES CLUB '10'

JANUARY 19th 1974 - WIMBLEDON - BELGRAVE 10 MILE CROSS COUNTRY CHAMP.

A superb run by James Rimmer took him to his first Belgrave Championship over road or country and the handicap prize to boot. He looked impressive over the initial circuit as he took a handy lead from Lionel Mann, with Laurie O'Hara and Colin Pearson strung out behind. Would he hold it though? We all know that Jim is capable of racing with the best but due to injuries and perhaps an occasionally too inhibited approach to his races, he does not always do himself justice. Lionel tenaciously fought back during laps two and three and the pressure was really on Jim as the gap narrowed. However, he was more than equal to the task and strode away with a brisk final lap to win the "Macher Shield" by a convincing margin. Well done James!

Colin Pearson again put in the sort of good work that fully deserves a championship medal but 4th place was his lot, and Laurie, after running the Mitcham '15' the previous week, seems to be on the road to recovery after his leg trouble.

Leading the 'cyclists' home came Les Morris and another to excel was John Baker who turned in his best ever time for the course.

items.heading: Tom Pritchard
items.summary: Obituary of Tom Pritchard, who died aged 66 after 50 years as a Belgrave member, Life Member, Vice President and assistant treasurer.
items.text:
Tom Pritchard

It is with great regret that we have to advise the death of Tom Pritchard who passed on at the age of 66 years. Tom joined the Club on the 10th June 1924, and I think he must have been the longest serving active member - 50 years.

Tom was never a champion but was known for his enthusiasm which he showed in Open and Club Handicaps, win or lose.

He was of a quiet disposition and would never push himself but was ever willing to help others either as Track or Field events official. During the last few years he had taken on the position as Assistant Treasurer. Due to his helpful nature Tom was elected a Life Member and a Vice President and would no doubt have been elected President in the near future. Tom was also a Past President and Life Member of the Veteran's Athletic Club. He will be missed by all.

We mourn one who has served the Club well and we offer our condolences to his wife Flo and daughter Jill and son Brian who is a member of Belgrave Harriers.

R.I.P.

F. R. Webb

items.heading: O'HARA AND BELS. 1ST
items.summary: Report and results of the National Veterans cross country championships at Great Barr, West Bromwich, on 24 February 1974, where Laurie O'Hara won the Class I title and Belgrave retained the San Sebastian Cup team award, with a page of photos by Al Rockall.
items.text:
O'HARA AND BELS. 1ST

FEBRUARY 24th 1974 - WEST BROMWICH - NATIONAL VETERANS C.C. CHAMPS.

Belgrave went to the National Veterans Cross Country Championships at Great Barr, West Bromwich, on 24th February as holders of the Class I title (40 - 49). Although the Club has a strong veterans section, only last year's three scorers and John Baker made the trip - but that was good enough for, once again, the Bels returned with the individual trophy and the impressive San Sebastian Cup for the team award.

The field was slightly depleted through changes of date and venue, but the Class I field of 140 still contained some tough opposition. Laurie O'Hara, who had shown a slight lapse in form in recent weeks, was out for revenge over his Southern victor, George Brown of Verlea, and both were hard on the tails of the leaders after a fast start. But it was not Brown that Laurie had to fear. New recruit to the ranks Peter Goodfellow of City of Stoke AC was making a determined bid for the title himself and soon found he was in a 20 yards lead. To make matters worse Laurie took a tumble and it was almost two laps gone before he closed on the tall, rangy runner from Stoke. For the final circuit, Laurie just sat 'under the armpit' of the leader and did his famous waiting act and, sure enough, with just 80 yards left he shot to the front for the first, but most important, time. It was a fine victory.

Meanwhile, the winner was getting plenty of support. Clive Shippen had moved through after a bad patch and had taken Pat Newall with him, and the two Belgravians steadily consolidated their positions for the rest of the race to finish 9th and 10th.

The team score of 20 points was even better than last year's record low of 29. Those with long memories will also be impressed by the Derby line-up which included internationals Peter Wilkinson (13th), Joe Keily (17th) and Ted Matley (45th) but who had to be content with 3rd place on this day. A pity we couldn't have done that when they ran in the English National 10 to 15 years ago!

THE 'NATIONAL'

MARCH 2nd 1974 - GRAVES PARK, SHEFFIELD.

In what was his last 'National' appearance, our Captain Gerry North still managed to be first Belgravian home although he did not have a very comfortable run. He was hoping for a position inside the first 50 and after the first small lap was lying in the 50 - 60's with John Bicourt in close attendance. Unfortunately, by the end of the second lap he was suffering from stomach cramp and was gradually dropping back. John had by now gone way back down the field, looking as if he would be a lot more comfortable on a tartan track rather than an undulating, snow patched course that was more than a little boggy in the dips. Lionel Mann had a particularly good run as did Leo Coy in his first 'big time' role and with about 600 runners behind him.

At the time of going to press we were unable to confirm our team placing but it was certainly well down in the twenties and although this sounds disappointing at first, it must be borne in mind that we were not the only ones to suffer by a long chalk. Coventry Godiva our rivals from the 60's were well down (with our old friend Mel Thorpe still making the team) and Reading and TVH were also out of the first ten. However, it could be the beginning of a lean spell for us on the country, and a time for building up again from scratch.

items.heading: BICOURT 4TH IN N.ZEALAND
items.summary: Account of John Bicourt's fourth place in the 3000 metres steeplechase at the British Commonwealth Games in Christchurch on 26 January 1974, his illness beforehand, his meeting with Arthur Lydiard and his plans.
items.text:
BICOURT 4TH IN N.ZEALAND

JANUARY 26th 1974 - CHRISTCHURCH, NEW ZEALAND

THE TENTH BRITISH COMMONWEALTH GAMES

What a line up the Commonwealth Games 3000 metres Steeplechase produced; Benjamin Jipcho the World Record holder, Amos Biwott the Mexico Olympic Champion, Evans Mogaka who was ranked sixth in the World in 1973, and amongst those from these Isles our own John Bicourt who so narrowly missed the British Record last year.

John suffered a throat infection at Christmas and it still hadn't cleared up as the 'Games' approached. The team doctor diagnosed the trouble as a touch of bronchitis and with only nine days to the race, advised no running for three to five days! Better prepared was John Davies the Thames Valley Harrier representing Wales. He was lucky enough to spend two weeks in Nairobi over Christmas, getting the sun to his muscles.

So the race was on. The Kenyans made the running with the Welshmen Davies and Hayward following. John, not feeling too confident after the doctor's advice, played it safe and kept back down the field. At the half-way mark Biwott was dropping back but our man was still running steadily in seventh place. Running the race of his life, Davies stepped up the pressure with two laps to go. By now John was up with Hayward about 40 metres behind the leaders.

Shortly after the 'bell' the incident occurred in which Mogaka and Davies fell, leaving Jipcho to run home comfortably. They were both soon up again and heading hard for the finish but John Bicourt too was now moving really fast, feeling that he had something left in him. He had overtaken Hayward with just over a lap left and by the time the finish was reached there was a margin of six seconds between them. Mogaka, just out of reach, crossed the line in the bronze medal position ahead of him.

John wasn't disappointed with the result. How could he be with his second best time, running out of season and with a slight lack of confidence due to the illness. But still, he finished so strongly that he is certain that he could have run a faster time if he had felt more sure of himself early in the race.

During the period of dispute that followed, he at no time considered that he would move up into a medal position with the possible disqualification of Davies. As far as John was concerned Davies had run a magnificent race and thoroughly deserved his second place come what may. Thankfully the race positions were upheld.

A trip to Mount Cook with Arthur Lydiard made some impression on John who states," He produces the winners so you've got to listen to the man".

John's training consists of running a regular 70 miles per week the majority of which is at a steady pace. He has not liked the idea of fast time trials over the flat, feeling that he wants to save it for the races that matter. Lydiard's men, however, may run a trial at 90% of full effort only a week before a major championship, and include infinitely more fartlek type running in their training.

Talking with the famous New Zealand coach has influenced John to the extent that he now badly wants to improve his times on the flat over 1500 metres and 5000 metres. His hurdling is acknowledged to be fine and if he can work up some real pace he is convinced that it will give him that bit more edge and the ability to take on and beat the very best. He hopes to run in the Surrey County 5000 metres Championship and if international Norman Morrison, the Scottish athlete with a Surrey qualification, turns out that could be quite a race.

John's target now for the 'chase - 8 minutes 20 seconds!

items.heading: THE FLYING TIGERS
items.summary: Humorous first-person account by a new member, 'Thumper', of winning the Boxing Day 2 miles handicap at Battersea Park in new Tiger shoes, with an editor's note.
items.text:
THE FLYING TIGERS

by Thumper

As Battersea Park is almost on my doorstep I was more or less pressed into running the Boxing Day 2 miles by all my mates. So, there I was - new Club vest, baggy track suit bottoms and without a clue as I had only been in the Belgrave Harriers a few weeks and all this was quite new to me. I managed to get hold of an official looking fellow who entered my name and collected my money. He asked me what my handicap was and well, I almost said, "these two legs". After a bit of a haggle I found myself on a line way down the track.

Also on the line were two very fit looking types, a young lad with a bandage round his leg and Charlie Manning our beloved President. I still did not really know what was going on except that two miles was a hell of a long way on a Boxing Day. Then I noticed a peculiar phenomenon. All the runners were facing the wrong way. It took me a little while to figure out that I was wrong and I then gently turned myself round (it being the day after Christmas I was still a trifle numb).

Well, there was a sort of GO or OFF or something and we were all away at a fair old trot. Now the last time I was on a running track was sports day in "Wings For Victory Week" 1944 but I soon got the hang of it and with six laps to go my feet were thumping quite well. However, it soon became evident that I was building up a terrible oxygen debt. Legs were alright but my breath was pumping in and out in short pants, pyjamas and a scarf. Just when I thought that the Almighty had mis-read the instructions when he made me and had left out a lung or two, the young lad with the bandage dropped out and Charlie dropped back just to see if he was OK and keep him company. Thus there I was running at a fair old totter in the slipstream of the two fit heathens and with about four laps to go.

Admittedly we were moving at a good doddle but I was feeling as if my lungs were going to burst although the rest of me was tonking over quite well. I pottered on and then one of the heathens 'packed' leaving two of us all alone in front with half the Club howling on our tails. Two laps left and I gathered up all my strength from mind, body and soul and staggered on 'eyeballs out'. I forgot about breathing and I must have looked a terrible sight judging by the amazed look on the officials' faces as into the last lap I sped. With my famous 'Thames Embankment sprint' I flashed across the finishing line. I did not realise I had won (modesty prevents me from revealing my time).

Coughing and spluttering at the finish like an old steam engine that has past its best, I gradually 'came to' and trotted back to the dressing room for a good shower, a light massage and a little powder on my feet. I was soon as good as new. An organiser chap said that I must collect my prize (a very nice glass vase) and I would very much like to thank all those who made the Boxing Day meeting possible.

But the best is yet to come, dear readers, for my mother had bought me a pair of lightweight Tiger running shoes for Christmas and I was trying them out for the first time in this race. Hence the title of this story. I must say they do make a difference from running round the streets of London in ex-WD army boots, Zatopek style!

Editor's Note: Could this new member be Belgrave's answer to the legendary Wilson and Alf Tupper (Britain's first four minute smiler)? Watch out for future developments.

YOUNG ATHLETES

Those of you who qualified for a AAA 5 Star badge last year and who have not previously received it, should find it enclosed with this magazine - congratulations once again.

As you know, the number of points required for a badge of a certain standard is higher in each age group. Make it your aim this year to at least attain the same level that you did last summer. You are going to have to go faster, higher and longer to do it but with another winter behind you now, there is no reason why you should not even jump up a grade.

Some of our Junior athletes are in for a bonus season this year. The AAA Rule regarding age groups has been amended and the upper end of the Junior age group has been extended to under 20 at midnight on December 31st. This brings us into line with the age groups used in European competitions.

You may have noticed that the name of this section has been changed to 'Young Athletes' and it will now cover results for our Juniors, Youths and Boys (Senior Boys and Junior Boys). Of couse the older ones amongst you will often be competing in our Senior competitions and these results will be found throughout the rest of the magazine.

Adrian Cook wins Youths Championship

DECEMBER 1st 1973 - WIMBLEDON COMMON.

This race promised to be a 'cracker' with Adrian Cook facing stiff opposition from new members Michael Manning and John Flynn. Unfortunately John came off his motor bike the day before and although he was not hurt, he was shaken and bruised, and understandably left the fight for first place to the other two.

When the field reached the Windmill on the outward stretch of the two and a half mile course, Adrian appeared to be breaking away and a mile later after climbing the hill from Queensmere he had a lead of about 20 yards. But now it was Michael's turn. Showing great strength over the final stages he took the lead and held it to the finish.

Tony Ambler ran well in 4th position, putting behind him Steve Walter[illegible] and Toby Staff, who both looked a little uncomfortable over the country and missing the track.

SURREY C. C. CHAMPS.

JANUARY 5th 1974 - GUILDFORD.

We had quite a good turn out this year with twelve Belgravians making the trip to Guildford for the Surrey County Championships. The going was very muddy indeed after torrential rain and some parts of the course looked more suitable for slalom canoe racing. Gary Budinger was at one point seen ploughing along waist deep! All our boys seemed to find the heavy going more than they bargained for but perhaps Stevie Walters, with just that little more experience of running than the others was the least affected as he led our Youth team in. In the Junior event Simon Holmes ran creditably but looked rather lonely with no other Belgravian to back him up.

items.heading: Pat Parker
items.summary: Obituary of J. (Pat) Parker, Belgrave's 1930s international, Empire Games 3 miles bronze medallist and fourth in the 1937 National.
items.text:
Pat Parker

Older members will be sorry to learn of the recent death of one of our international stars of the 'thirties' J. (Pat) Parker.

When he joined us he was already an Empire Games Bronze Medallist (London 1934) at 3 miles. He lived at Brighton yet rarely missed not only the Saturday race or training run but the Tuesday and Thursday training runs from the Rising Sun, Ebury Bridge Road. He was a Sussex County Champion and put up many fine performances for us over the country, on the track and in road relays. Perhaps his best effort for us was when he finished fourth in the 'National' at Stratford Upon Avon in 1937.

To him life and running was fun - a great Club Character.

G. S. Doubleday
